articles.title: ‘I Come in Here Prepared to Die
articles.caption: The raucous underground Bronx boxing operation Knuckle Up...
articles.article: It\’s pouring rain in the Bronx. Inside, above an empty garage near the East River, I watch on as abuelitas and cauliflower-eared tough guys set up chairs, prep catering trays full of taquitos, and build a boxing ring from sailing rope and martial arts punching bags. Chase pulls me aside for a last-minute update: One of his fighters has \“broken his dick\”. \“This is the seventh or eighth time,” Chase tells me, laughing to himself in disbelief. The injury threatens to upend a long night of unsanctioned boxing matches, which Chase organizes, promotes, and even sometimes referees himself. He created Knuckle Up Fight Klub (Knuckle Up, for short) as a way for men and women from across New York City\’s five boroughs and beyond to settle their issues or develop their pugilistic skills in the ring. In doing so offering them an outlet away from the gun violence that has long plagued the city\’s northernmost borough. Though violent crime is at record lows in New York, the Bronx has long been the city\’s worst borough for gun violence, in 2025 accounting for more than a third of all shooting incidents and victims across the city. Chase thinks boxing can help fix that. “ We try to tell kids guns kill,” Chase says as the night’s crowd starts to pour in. He and his crew are adorned in black shirts with a pink fist emblazoned on the front. He’s wearing leather pants with a wallet chain, and his crisp faux-hawk lined up to perfection. “ Put the guns down and do what we used to do: knuckle up.” Knuckle Up offers the community two separate but related opportunities, Chase says. The fights give aspiring young boxers, the kind who may go on to have amateur or even professional careers, a showcase for their skills; untrained laymen, on the other hand, the chance to work out their violent urges in a slightly more controlled but far less deadly environment than they may find in the streets. Knuckle Up events will often feature “beef fights,” Chase tells me, where two people are given the opportunity to settle real-world disagreements inside the squared circle. “ If we can help somebody and inspire them to, like, either want to go pro or go amateur, great,” Chase says. “But [Knuckle Up] is also for those that know for a fact they ain’t going to make it nowhere in boxing but still need to get shit off their chest and want to come handle their business.” The Bronx has hosted underground boxing for years. But Chase says that the scene has long catered mostly to nightlife, with venues often filled with hookah smoke and exotic dancers. Chase first began promoting Knuckle Up over seven years ago, splitting off from another underground boxing promotion outfit to create an event where no gambling, dancers, or smoking is allowed, allowing the fighters to fight—and breathe—free of distraction. Chase recalls one of Knuckle Up’s earliest events, from around 2020, when he says he organized an event around a fight between two reputed gang members who had been feuding over a woman. One, he says, was a member of a Bloods set, and the other a Crips set, two groups that have been at the center of one of longest tenured and most well known gang disputes in American history. Chase tells me that he was able to intervene in the dispute via phone, and invited both to duke it out and settle their beef at Knuckle Up. Following the match, he says that both the Bloods and Crips sets lingered in front of the venue, held at bay by the security that Knuckle Up events have come to employ. “Every event I’m scared, because we’re not sanctioned, and if anything really pops off or if someone gets hurt I know that it’s gonna be on me,” Chase says. (This is also the reason that Chase has asked for us to use only his first name for this story.) Once setup is complete, security beckons attendees through a dilapidated hallway, scanning guests for weapons. The room quickly fills to a crowd of about 100. Tweens and 20-somethings with face tattoos and middle-aged people alike file in and shuffle to their seats, while rap and reggaeton blares in the background at a volume seemingly designed to deafen. One attendee walks in holding a newborn baby. Knuckle Up is not without grit. As the night goes on, more technical, journeyman boxing matches give way to fights closer to street brawls. Fighters with names like Hot Hands Hollis and “Busta” Douglas stand forehead to forehead with their opponents, throwing haymakers. Blood stains begin to collect on the inch-thick mats separating boxers from the concrete floor. In a billed “retirement fight,” a competitor boxing under the name “Loso” bludgeons his opponent in his braces so severely that the fight is called on account of the bleeding. Chase tells me that Loso had been at the center of a long-running street beef with another Knuckle Up fighter for years, one that threatened to boil over into street violence but which Chase was able to curtail in a series of three fights. (Loso lost all of them.) In one of the night’s co–main events, Chase's aforementioned broken-dicked fighter, a stout, muscular man in glistening white satin shorts courageously takes to the ring. The match begins promisingly, but after a few quick exchanges, a painfully low blow straight to the broken dick ends the fight in the first round, prompting boos from the crowd. “Underground” is not marketing-speak—Knuckle Up is totally unregulated. One fight, which ended with a victor, was given an extra round at the behest of a rowdy audience. In another, the judges could not reach an agreement on the winner. Chase and I also disagreed on the result. Authorized boxing matches in New York State require approval from a state athletic commission and one of the sports’ sanctioning bodies, like the WBA and IBO for professionals. This process can cost hundreds or even thousands of dollars (many professional governing bodies take 3% of fighters’ purses). Sometimes fighters have to pay membership and insurance fees. They are also required to obtain medical approval to fight, including a physical and even occasional blood work—which can add up to hundreds of dollars. Edwin “Tatequieto” Santana, a boxing coach based in the Bronx who corners 12 boxers the night I attend, tells me that cost is prohibitive for many of the young fighters that he coaches. “This is an avenue to get the experience, the exposure,” Santana says. But medical oversight can also save lives. At formally sanctioned boxing events, doctors are on premises in case of emergencies and to examine fighters before and after competition. These examinations can and have prevented the deaths of fighters who have received traumatic brain injuries in the past. The final fight kicks off minutes to midnight, as children and grandparents begin to trickle toward the exit. Raji ends the night quickly with a straight right that sends his opponent careening into the ropes; the other fighter is seemingly unconscious before he hits the ground. His head lands inches from the exposed concrete, nearly in my seat. I look into his vacant, glazed-over eyes, and watch his jaw clench, his hands jutting awkwardly out in front of him—what appears to be the “fencing response,” an involuntary reaction that is a telltale sign of a brain injury. Raji’s corner and friends storm the ring celebrating, while his opponent, still struggling to stand yet insisting he’s fine. Raji briefly breaks away from rejoicing to check on the fighter on the ground, who is eventually escorted out with the help of his coaches. Minutes later, Raji is talking to me about the realities of prizefighting. “ I know CTE is a real thing, and stuff like that is how people get significant CTE,” he says. “ One of us could possibly die in this ring,  and truth be told—maybe it’s selfish on my end—I come in here prepared to die.”

articles.title: TurnStyle Launches to Spotlight New York City's Underground Boxing Scene
articles.caption: Take a ride on NYS'c craziest ride...
articles.article: A new platform is stepping into the ring with a mission to elevate New York City's underground boxing community. TurnStyle is a digital hub dedicated to covering, showcasing, and preserving the stories, athletes, and events that make up the city's thriving local fight scene. Built for fighters, promoters, and fans alike, TurnStyle aims to become the central destination for discovering the next generation of boxing talent. Launching with partnerships alongside four established event promoters, TurnStyle provides a unified platform where local organizations can promote upcoming fight cards, share event coverage, and expand their reach to a broader audience. By bringing multiple promotions together under one roof, the platform creates greater visibility for the athletes who dedicate themselves to the sport. For fighters, TurnStyle offers more than exposure. The platform maintains organized fight records, athlete profiles, media galleries, and event history, allowing competitors to build a professional digital portfolio throughout their careers. Whether seeking sponsorships, larger fight opportunities, or recognition from gyms and promoters, fighters can use TurnStyle to showcase both their accomplishments and their journey. The platform also introduces new opportunities for revenue and fan engagement. Fighters and promoters will be able to sell official merchandise, promote future events, and offer tickets directly through the site. This creates additional ways for supporters to invest in the athletes and organizations they believe in while strengthening the local boxing community. At its core, TurnStyle exists to document a culture that often goes unnoticed. Every event, every victory, and every competitor contributes to the history of New York City's boxing scene. By combining media coverage, organized records, event promotion, and athlete cataloging into a single destination, TurnStyle is building an archive for today's fighters while creating opportunities for tomorrow's champions. The goal is simple: give New York City's underground boxing community the visibility, recognition, and support it deserves.
